title: Filling station
description: Facility that sells gasoline and diesel
wiki_lead:
A filling station (also known as a gas station [US/CA] or petrol station [UK/AU/NZ]) is a facility that sells fuel and engine lubricants for motor vehicles. It serves as a local fuel depot and retailer; it receives fuel products from refineries (via regular tank truck resupplies), stores the fuels in (typically underground) storage tanks, and distributes the fuel to motorist consumers at a daily varied price.
The most common fuels sold are motor fuels such as gasoline (petrol), often as multiple products with different octane ratings) and diesel fuel, as well as liquified petroleum gas (LPG, i.e. autogas), compressed natural gas, compressed hydrogen, hydrogen compressed natural gas, liquid hydrogen, kerosene, alcohol fuels (like methanol, ethanol, butanol, and propanol), biofuels (like straight vegetable oil and biodiesel), or other types of alternative fuels. Fuel dispensers are used to pump fuel into the vehicle's fuel tanks, gauge the volume of fuel transferred to the vehicle, and calculate the amount the consumer must pay. Another device found in filling stations and capable of refueling certain (compressed-air) vehicles is an air compressor. However, these are generally used to inflate car tires. 
Many filling stations provide convenience stores, which may sell convenience food, beverages, tobacco products, lottery tickets, newspapers, magazines, and, in some cases, a small selection of grocery items, such as milk or eggs. Some also sell propane or butane and have added shops to their primary business. Conversely, some chain stores, such as supermarkets, discount stores, warehouse clubs, or traditional convenience stores, have provided fuel pumps on the site.

Terminology

In North America, the colloquial generic term for motor fuels is "gasoline" or "gas" for short due to gasoline engines being the most ubiquitous car internal combustion engine, and the terms "gas station" and "service station" are used in the United States, Canada, and the Caribbean. In some regions of Canada, the term "gas bar" (or "gasbar") is used. 
In the rest of the English-speaking world, the generic term for fuel is "petrol". Since 1860, Carless, Capel & Leonard of Hackney Wick, London had been making a petroleum distillate with specific gravity 0.68 as a mineral oil solvent. In the 1890s, Frederick Simms found that this distillate was ideal for Daimler's engines and suggested to Carless that they adopt "Petrol" as its brand name, which they did. Carless was unable to defend it as a trademark: in 1902 John Scott Montagu said that it was "always called amongst motorists 'petrol' and Gottlieb Daimler said that the term had been in use in England in the 1860s. 
Thus the terms "petrol station" and "petrol pump" are used in the United Kingdom. In Ireland, New Zealand and South Africa "garage" and "forecourt" are still commonly used. Similarly, in Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and Ireland, the term "service station" describes any petrol station; Australians also call it a "servo". In India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, it is called a "petrol pump" or a "petrol bunk". In Japanese, a commonly used term is gasoline stand although the abbreviation SS (for service station) is also used.


History

In the early days of the internal-combustion engine, fuel for motor vehicles was sold in the same way as similar liquids, e.g. organic solvents, which is what the first motor fuel, Ligroin, was. That is why, when Bertha Benz wanted to refill the tank of the first automobile on her trip from Mannheim to Pforzheim in 1888, she visited the pharmacy in Wiesloch, where she bought Ligroin. 
As the motor trade developed and standard products were adopted as fuels, businesses developed to support motorists by offering repair services and holding stocks of fuel for sale. 
The first filling station, as now understood, appears to have been that opened in 1905 at 420, South Theresa Avenue, St. Louis, Missouri, USA.

grok_lead: A filling station, also known as a gas station or petrol station, is a retail facility that sells fuels such as gasoline, diesel, and sometimes liquefied petroleum gas primarily for motor vehicle s, along with engine lubricants and related automotive products. These establishments feature fuel dispensers connected to underground storage tanks, payment terminals, and often an integrated convenience store providing snacks, beverages, and minor vehicle maintenance items. Emerging in the early 20th century with the proliferation of automobiles, the first purpose-built drive-in filling station opened in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 1913, marking a shift from curbside or pharmacy-based fuel sales to dedicated infrastructure. By the 1920s, major oil companies standardized operations, incorporating services like tire inflation and oil changes, while self-service modelsâfirst introduced in 1947âbecame widespread by the 1970s, driven by cost efficiencies and consumer adoption in regions permitting it. Today, filling stations adapt to regulatory demands for safety features like automatic shutoff nozzles and spill prevention, alongside evolving fuel options including biofuels and emerging hydrogen or electric charging in select locations, though petroleum derivatives remain dominant due to infrastructure scale and vehicle fleet realities.
